screens.title: Parameters, Arguments, and Return Values
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we'll make the flow of data in and out of functions clear and practical. You will learn the difference between parameters — the named placeholders a function declares — and arguments — the actual values supplied when the function is called. We’ll show how positional arguments match parameters by order, how keyword arguments let you name values for clarity, and how default parameter values provide sensible fallbacks. You will also see how a single return can package multiple results as a tuple and how to unpack those results into variables. The examples you’ll study include a pet description function and a BMI calculator, so you get both syntax and real use cases. Understanding these patterns reduces bugs from swapped values, makes calls more readable, and helps you design flexible functions. As you move through the lessons, notice the small differences that change meaning, practice unpacking returned tuples, and ask yourself how each function’s signature signals correct usage.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Overview
Parameters, Arguments, and Return Values
A practical guide to passing data into functions and getting results back
In this lesson

Differentiate parameters and arguments. Practice positional and keyword styles. Use defaults. Return and unpack multiple values as tuples.

Why it matters

Clear signatures make code readable, prevent logical errors from swapped inputs, and let you design functions that are easy to call and reuse.

How to use this chapter

Follow examples, run the provided code snippets, and try the BMI activity to practice defaults and unpacking returns.

Explore Key Topics
Positional vs Keyword
Order matters for positional; naming removes order dependency.
Default parameters
Provide common values so callers can omit arguments safely.
Returning tuples
Package several values in one return and unpack at the call site.

Arguments flow into parameters; functions send results back

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of these lessons you will clearly tell parameters and arguments apart, use positional and keyword arguments confidently, set default parameter values to simplify calls, and return multiple values as a tuple. Each objective is practical: you will inspect function signatures to spot expected inputs, reorder calls safely with keywords, provide sensible defaults when many callers share common values, and design returns that package several results for easy unpacking. For example, when you see def describe_pet(animal_type, pet_name) you will know those names are parameters; calling describe_pet('hamster','harry') supplies arguments. You will also practice the rule that positional arguments precede keyword arguments so you avoid syntax errors. Finally, you will write and test a BMI function that uses defaults and returns a numeric result, and a user-info example that returns a name and age together so you can unpack them into separate variables. These skills make your functions readable and reduce logic bugs.

screens.title: Parameters vs Arguments
screens.narratorSegment: Let's define parameters and arguments so they never get mixed up. A parameter is the named placeholder in a function definition. It declares what the function expects and creates a local variable for use inside the function. An argument is the concrete value you provide when you call the function. That value is assigned to the corresponding parameter for the duration of the call. For example, in a function defined as def describe_pet(animal_type, pet_name): animal_type and pet_name are parameters. When you call describe_pet('hamster', 'harry') the strings 'hamster' and 'harry' are arguments. A helpful mental model is: parameters are variable names on a form; arguments are the answers you write on that form. A common misconception is to call parameters "inputs" and arguments "parameters" interchangeably. This slips up debugging because you might change the call when the error is actually in the signature. To test your understanding, look at a function signature and ask: which names are declared here? Then look at a call and ask: which actual values are being supplied? Try swapping the argument order in the describe_pet call and notice how the printed result changes — that demonstrates the difference clearly. What will you check first when a function prints unexpected values?

keyIdea.text: Parameters declare names in a function signature; arguments are values supplied when calling that function.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Parameters vs Arguments
Clear definitions
  • Parameter: the name listed in a function definition, a local variable placeholder.
  • Argument: the actual value supplied when calling the function, assigned to the parameter.
  • Mental model: parameter = slot, argument = thing you put into the slot.
Example
def describe_pet(animal_type, pet_name):
    print(f"I have a {animal_type}.")
    print(f"My {animal_type}'s name is {pet_name.title()}.")

# animal_type and pet_name are parameters
# 'hamster' and 'harry' are arguments
describe_pet('hamster', 'harry')
Key Takeaway

When debugging, check whether the mistake is in the parameter names or the arguments supplied; they are distinct responsibilities.

Common misconception

People sometimes call arguments "parameters" and vice versa. This confusion leads to changing the wrong part of the code. Always map signature names to call values to avoid this error.

Try this
Swap the two arguments in the example and observe how the meaning changes even though the code still runs. That shows parameters control meaning, not execution.
Why it matters

Distinguishing them helps you write clearer APIs and prevents silent logical errors caused by swapped values or incorrect assumptions about what a function expects.

screens.title: Positional Arguments
screens.narratorSegment: Positional arguments are the simplest way to pass values: Python matches each provided value to a parameter by position. This is compact and natural when the order is obvious. For example, describe_pet('hamster', 'harry') assigns 'hamster' to the first parameter and 'harry' to the second. The important point is that the order determines meaning. If you reverse the arguments and call describe_pet('harry', 'hamster'), the program still runs but prints incorrect, misleading messages. That kind of bug is logical rather than syntactic, and can be subtle in larger functions with many parameters. To avoid such mistakes, use positional arguments when the meaning is very clear and short. When a function has many parameters or parameters of the same type, positional calls become risky. A quick test you can do is to re-run a call using keyword arguments: if the output is the same, the original positional order was correct; if not, you uncovered a hidden assumption. Ask yourself: does the order communicate intent clearly, or will readers benefit from named arguments? Positional Arguments means positional arguments assign values by order; convenient but error-prone when many similar parameters exist.. In practical terms, order-based matching of arguments to parameters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Positional Arguments
Two examples: correct and swapped
Correct order
describe_pet('hamster', 'harry')
# prints: I have a hamster. My hamster's name is Harry.
Swapped order (logical bug)
describe_pet('harry', 'hamster')
# prints misleading sentences even though code runs
Guidance

Prefer positional for short functions where parameter order is obvious. For longer signatures, prefer keywords to avoid accidental swaps.

Supporting notes
  • Positional calls are concise and common for simple functions.
  • They produce logical errors if you misorder values of the same type.
  • To verify intent, rewrite a positional call as a keyword call and compare outputs.
Check your understanding

If two parameters both expect strings, what will a swapped positional call usually cause: a SyntaxError, a TypeError, or a logical mistake in output?

screens.title: Keyword Arguments
screens.narratorSegment: Keyword arguments let you pass values by naming the parameter explicitly in the call. This makes calls self-documenting and order-independent. For example, describe_pet(pet_name='harry', animal_type='hamster') produces the same printed output as the positional call but is clearer about which value maps to which parameter. This clarity is especially helpful when functions take many parameters or optional settings. Keyword arguments also make reordering in code safe. You can place the arguments in any sequence and Python still matches them by name. However, remember that positional arguments must come first in a mixed call. Another useful pattern is to use keyword arguments at the call site when you override default values for selected parameters. A misconception is thinking keywords are slower or somehow less Pythonic; in fact they are widely encouraged when they improve readability. Practice converting a positional call to a keyword call and observe how the meaning becomes explicit. Do you see places in your code where named parameters would prevent subtle bugs? Keyword Arguments means keyword arguments name parameter assignments so order no longer determines meaning; they improve readability and reduce swapped-value bugs.. In practical terms, naming values to remove dependency on order. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Keyword Arguments
Example: named arguments
describe_pet(pet_name='harry', animal_type='hamster')
# order does not matter; naming ensures correct mapping
When to use

Prefer keywords for functions with many parameters, optional settings, or when values are not naturally ordered. They make calls self-documenting.

Mixing with positional args

You can combine positional and keyword arguments, but positional ones must appear first. For example, describe_pet('cat', pet_name='whiskers') is valid. Reversing that order causes a syntax error.

Common misconception

Keywords are not less efficient; they are a readability tool. Use them where they reduce ambiguity.

Check

Convert a positional call with three parameters into a keyword call. Does the output match? If not, what changed?

screens.title: Mixing Positional and Keyword Arguments
screens.narratorSegment: Mixing styles is common and useful, but there is a simple rule to follow: any positional arguments must come before keyword arguments in the same call. This rule exists because Python initially assigns values by position, then fills named parameters. For example, describe_pet('cat', pet_name='whiskers') is valid because the positional 'cat' fills the first parameter, and the named pet_name fills the second. However, writing describe_pet(pet_name='whiskers', 'cat') is a syntax error because the interpreter cannot accept a positional value after a keyword assignment. A recommended pattern is to place required positional arguments first, then optional or clearly named arguments as keywords. This makes calls readable and prevents syntax errors. When you design function signatures, group required parameters first, then parameters with defaults. That aligns natural usage with the language rule and keeps callers from needing to remember surprising ordering. As a quick exercise, reorder a mixed call incorrectly to see the syntax error, then fix it by moving the positional value before named arguments. Mixing Positional and Keyword Arguments means positional arguments must appear before keyword arguments; design signatures so required parameters come first.. In practical terms, rules and safe usage patterns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Mixing Arguments
Rule illustrated
Valid: describe_pet('cat', pet_name='whiskers')
Invalid: describe_pet(pet_name='whiskers', 'cat') — SyntaxError
Design tip

Place required parameters first, then optional parameters with defaults. Callers can then use simple positional calls for required data and keywords for optional overrides.

Supporting steps
  1. Read the function signature to identify required vs defaulted parameters.
  2. Call with positional values for required parameters only.
  3. Use keyword arguments to override specific default parameters as needed.
Check your understanding

If a function defines def f(a, b=2, c=3): is f(1, c=5) valid? Try it and explain why.

screens.title: Default Parameter Values
screens.narratorSegment: Default parameter values let you specify a value that a parameter will take when the caller omits that argument. This reduces verbosity for common cases and makes the A P I easier to use. For example, in def describe_pet_default(pet_name, animal_type='dog'): the parameter animal_type defaults to the string 'dog' if not supplied. Calling describe_pet_default(pet_name='willie') uses the default. If the caller provides animal_type explicitly, that value overrides the default. Defaults are evaluated at function definition time, so avoid using mutable objects like lists or dictionaries as defaults unless you understand the implications. A common misconception is that defaults are only for optional parameters; they are designed for parameters that commonly have a sensible value. When you design defaults, pick values that reflect the most frequent case, and document what happens when callers override them. Practice writing a function with a default and calling it both with and without the argument to observe the override behavior. What default would you pick for a timezone parameter in a logging function? Default Parameter Values means set defaults in the signature to provide sensible values when callers omit arguments; explicit arguments override defaults.. In practical terms, providing fallbacks in function signatures. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Default Parameter Values
Example
def describe_pet_default(pet_name, animal_type='dog'):
    print(f"I have a {animal_type}.")
    print(f"My {animal_type}'s name is {pet_name.title()}.")

describe_pet_default(pet_name='willie')  # uses default 'dog'
describe_pet_default(pet_name='harry', animal_type='hamster')  # overrides default
Design considerations
  • Choose defaults that reflect the common case to simplify callers.
  • Avoid mutable default objects unless you intentionally want shared state.
  • Document defaults so callers understand what is assumed.
Check

Call a function with and without a defaulted parameter to confirm which value gets used. How does overriding work?

screens.title: Overriding Defaults and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Overriding defaults is straightforward: provide an argument for that parameter in the call and Python uses the supplied value instead of the default. Use overrides when the caller needs a behavior different from the common case. A good practice is to design your signature so defaults capture typical, safe behavior and overrides are explicit, visible, and easy to understand. For example, if a function logs events and defaults to a 'UTC' timezone, callers who need local times can pass timezone='local' to override the default. When mixing overrides with positional values, use keyword arguments for the overrides to make intent clear. Another helpful habit is to keep defaulted parameters at the end of the parameter list, which aligns with the positional-before-keyword rule and keeps required data first. A misconception is to assume defaults hide complexity; actually, they simplify common use but callers must still be able to override when special cases appear. When you test functions, include at least one call that relies on the default and one that overrides it to ensure both paths behave correctly. What default values in your functions would make most calls simpler?

keyIdea.title: Override pattern
keyIdea.text: Provide explicit arguments to override defaults; design defaults for common use and keep them last in the signature.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Overriding Defaults
Pattern: defaults then overrides
  • Place defaults after required parameters so calls remain natural.
  • Use keyword arguments to override defaults for clarity.
  • Test both default and override paths in your code.
Example override
def display(value, format='text'):
    # default behaviour
    pass

# override default format
display(123, format='json')
Supporting guidance

Avoid hidden side effects in defaults. If a default triggers heavy work, consider making that behavior explicit to the caller to avoid surprising performance costs.

Pro tip

When in doubt, prefer a clear explicit parameter over a complex implicit default. Simpler calls are easier to reason about later.

screens.title: Returning Multiple Values as a Tuple
screens.narratorSegment: A function can return multiple related values by returning them together in a single data structure. The most common and idiomatic choice in Python is the tuple. When you write return full_name, age Python automatically packs those items into a tuple. The important nuance is that while a function executes one return statement per call, that return can contain many items grouped into one object. Using tuples for multiple returns keeps the interface lightweight and predictable. For example, get_user_info('john','doe',30) might return a tuple ('John Doe', 30). You can assign the returned tuple to a single variable to inspect or print it, or you can unpack it into separate variables for immediate use. Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › BMI Activity
Starter code
def calculate_bmi(weight_kg, height_m, unit='metric'):
    """
    Calculates BMI given weight in kg and height in meters.
    Unit parameter is for demonstration of default values.
    """
    bmi = weight_kg / (height_m ** 2)
    return bmi

# Example calls shown on the right
Example calls
# Positional
bmi1 = calculate_bmi(70, 1.75)
print(f"BMI (positional): {bmi1}")

# Keyword
bmi2 = calculate_bmi(height_m=1.80, weight_kg=85, unit='imperial')
print(f"BMI (keyword): {bmi2}")

# Default unit
bmi3 = calculate_bmi(65, 1.60)
print(f"BMI (default unit): {bmi3}")

# Override unit
bmi4 = calculate_bmi(65, 1.60, unit='imperial')
print(f"BMI (override unit): {bmi4}")
Check

Run each call and confirm identical numeric results for metric calls; the unit parameter demonstrates overriding but doesn't affect calculation here.

screens.title: Common Errors and Debugging Tips
screens.narratorSegment: Be aware of two common classes of errors when working with parameters and arguments. The first is logical errors: the code runs but produces incorrect results because values were swapped or the wrong parameter was given a value. For example, swapping positional arguments in describe_pet produces misleading output. To debug, rewrite the call using keyword arguments to see which mapping produces the intended result. The second is syntax errors from mixing argument styles incorrectly; placing a positional argument after a keyword argument raises a SyntaxError, which the interpreter flags immediately. Another frequent mistake is using mutable objects as default parameter values, which can create shared state across calls; avoid this pattern unless you intentionally want that behavior. Good debugging habits include reading signatures before calls, running small test calls with explicit keywords to validate behavior, and documenting defaults in docstrings. When unpacking returns, ensure the number of variables matches the tuple length. These small checks catch many bugs early. As a final check, ask: did a failing example raise an exception or just produce wrong output? The answer tells you whether to check syntax or argument meaning.

Logical errors (silent)

Swapping positional arguments produces wrong output without raising an exception. Verify by calling with keywords to see the intended mapping.

Avoid lists or dicts as default parameters unless you intentionally want shared state across calls. Use None and create a new object inside the function instead.

screens.title: Designing Clear Function Signatures
screens.narratorSegment: Designing function signatures with clarity in mind prevents many of the problems we discussed. A useful pattern is to group parameters by role: required positional parameters first, then optional parameters with defaults, and finally keyword-only options if your A P I needs them. Keeping related parameters contiguous helps readers understand what values are essential and what are configurational. Document defaults in the docstring so callers know when they can omit arguments. For returned values, if you return multiple items with fixed meaning, a tuple is fine. If the returned pieces are numerous or benefit from named access, consider returning a dictionary or small object for clarity. A common misconception is to overload a function signature with many optional flags; instead, prefer a small, well-documented signature or split responsibilities across helper functions. When you review a signature, ask whether a caller can tell what to pass without reading the body. If not, revise names or add sensible defaults. This habit leads to code that is easier to use and less likely to suffer accidental misuse. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we'll make the flow of data in and out of functions clear and practical. You will learn the difference between parameters — the named placeholders a function declares — and arguments — the actual values supplied when the function is called. We’ll show how positional arguments match parameters by order, how keyword arguments let you name values for clarity, and how default parameter values provide sensible fallbacks. You will also see how a single return can package multiple results as a tuple and how to unpack those results into variables. The examples you’ll study include a pet description function and a BMI calculator, so you get both syntax and real use cases. Understanding these patterns reduces bugs from swapped values, makes calls more readable, and helps you design flexible functions. As you move through the lessons, notice the small differences that change meaning, practice unpacking returned tuples, and ask yourself how each function’s signature signals correct usage.

By the end of these lessons you will clearly tell parameters and arguments apart, use positional and keyword arguments confidently, set default parameter values to simplify calls, and return multiple values as a tuple. Each objective is practical: you will inspect function signatures to spot expected inputs, reorder calls safely with keywords, provide sensible defaults when many callers share common values, and design returns that package several results for easy unpacking. For example, when you see def describe_pet(animal_type, pet_name) you will know those names are parameters; calling describe_pet('hamster','harry') supplies arguments. You will also practice the rule that positional arguments precede keyword arguments so you avoid syntax errors. Finally, you will write and test a BMI function that uses defaults and returns a numeric result, and a user-info example that returns a name and age together so you can unpack them into separate variables. These skills make your functions readable and reduce logic bugs.

These practice goals focus on concrete behaviors: read a function signature and list its parameters; call functions with positional arguments and then rewrite the same calls using keywords to show identical results; change and remove arguments to see default values take effect; and return two values from a function and unpack them into separate variables. For example, you will call the describe_pet function both as describe_pet('hamster','harry') and as describe_pet(pet_name='harry', animal_type='hamster') to confirm identical printed output. For return practice, you will write get_user_info that returns a formatted name and age, assign the returned tuple to a variable and then unpack it into name and years. These deliberate exercises build muscle memory and help you spot common mistakes like swapped positional arguments or forgetting that positional arguments must come before keywords. Learning Objectives — Practice Goals means read signatures, call with both styles, test defaults, return and unpack tuples to build robust habits.. In practical terms, skills you will practice and demonstrate. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's define parameters and arguments so they never get mixed up. A parameter is the named placeholder in a function definition. It declares what the function expects and creates a local variable for use inside the function. An argument is the concrete value you provide when you call the function. That value is assigned to the corresponding parameter for the duration of the call. For example, in a function defined as def describe_pet(animal_type, pet_name): animal_type and pet_name are parameters. When you call describe_pet('hamster', 'harry') the strings 'hamster' and 'harry' are arguments. A helpful mental model is: parameters are variable names on a form; arguments are the answers you write on that form. A common misconception is to call parameters "inputs" and arguments "parameters" interchangeably. This slips up debugging because you might change the call when the error is actually in the signature. To test your understanding, look at a function signature and ask: which names are declared here? Then look at a call and ask: which actual values are being supplied? Try swapping the argument order in the describe_pet call and notice how the printed result changes — that demonstrates the difference clearly. What will you check first when a function prints unexpected values?

Positional arguments are the simplest way to pass values: Python matches each provided value to a parameter by position. This is compact and natural when the order is obvious. For example, describe_pet('hamster', 'harry') assigns 'hamster' to the first parameter and 'harry' to the second. The important point is that the order determines meaning. If you reverse the arguments and call describe_pet('harry', 'hamster'), the program still runs but prints incorrect, misleading messages. That kind of bug is logical rather than syntactic, and can be subtle in larger functions with many parameters. To avoid such mistakes, use positional arguments when the meaning is very clear and short. When a function has many parameters or parameters of the same type, positional calls become risky. A quick test you can do is to re-run a call using keyword arguments: if the output is the same, the original positional order was correct; if not, you uncovered a hidden assumption. Ask yourself: does the order communicate intent clearly, or will readers benefit from named arguments? Positional Arguments means positional arguments assign values by order; convenient but error-prone when many similar parameters exist.. In practical terms, order-based matching of arguments to parameters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Keyword arguments let you pass values by naming the parameter explicitly in the call. This makes calls self-documenting and order-independent. For example, describe_pet(pet_name='harry', animal_type='hamster') produces the same printed output as the positional call but is clearer about which value maps to which parameter. This clarity is especially helpful when functions take many parameters or optional settings. Keyword arguments also make reordering in code safe. You can place the arguments in any sequence and Python still matches them by name. However, remember that positional arguments must come first in a mixed call. Another useful pattern is to use keyword arguments at the call site when you override default values for selected parameters. A misconception is thinking keywords are slower or somehow less Pythonic; in fact they are widely encouraged when they improve readability. Practice converting a positional call to a keyword call and observe how the meaning becomes explicit. Do you see places in your code where named parameters would prevent subtle bugs? Keyword Arguments means keyword arguments name parameter assignments so order no longer determines meaning; they improve readability and reduce swapped-value bugs.. In practical terms, naming values to remove dependency on order. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Mixing styles is common and useful, but there is a simple rule to follow: any positional arguments must come before keyword arguments in the same call. This rule exists because Python initially assigns values by position, then fills named parameters. For example, describe_pet('cat', pet_name='whiskers') is valid because the positional 'cat' fills the first parameter, and the named pet_name fills the second. However, writing describe_pet(pet_name='whiskers', 'cat') is a syntax error because the interpreter cannot accept a positional value after a keyword assignment. A recommended pattern is to place required positional arguments first, then optional or clearly named arguments as keywords. This makes calls readable and prevents syntax errors. When you design function signatures, group required parameters first, then parameters with defaults. That aligns natural usage with the language rule and keeps callers from needing to remember surprising ordering. As a quick exercise, reorder a mixed call incorrectly to see the syntax error, then fix it by moving the positional value before named arguments. Mixing Positional and Keyword Arguments means positional arguments must appear before keyword arguments; design signatures so required parameters come first.. In practical terms, rules and safe usage patterns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Default parameter values let you specify a value that a parameter will take when the caller omits that argument. This reduces verbosity for common cases and makes the A P I easier to use. For example, in def describe_pet_default(pet_name, animal_type='dog'): the parameter animal_type defaults to the string 'dog' if not supplied. Calling describe_pet_default(pet_name='willie') uses the default. If the caller provides animal_type explicitly, that value overrides the default. Defaults are evaluated at function definition time, so avoid using mutable objects like lists or dictionaries as defaults unless you understand the implications. A common misconception is that defaults are only for optional parameters; they are designed for parameters that commonly have a sensible value. When you design defaults, pick values that reflect the most frequent case, and document what happens when callers override them. Overriding defaults is straightforward: provide an argument for that parameter in the call and Python uses the supplied value instead of the default. Use overrides when the caller needs a behavior different from the common case. A good practice is to design your signature so defaults capture typical, safe behavior and overrides are explicit, visible, and easy to understand. For example, if a function logs events and defaults to a 'UTC' timezone, callers who need local times can pass timezone='local' to override the default. When mixing overrides with positional values, use keyword arguments for the overrides to make intent clear. Another helpful habit is to keep defaulted parameters at the end of the parameter list, which aligns with the positional-before-keyword rule and keeps required data first. A misconception is to assume defaults hide complexity; actually, they simplify common use but callers must still be able to override when special cases appear. When you test functions, include at least one call that relies on the default and one that overrides it to ensure both paths behave correctly. A function can return multiple related values by returning them together in a single data structure. The most common and idiomatic choice in Python is the tuple. When you write return full_name, age Python automatically packs those items into a tuple. The important nuance is that while a function executes one return statement per call, that return can contain many items grouped into one object. Using tuples for multiple returns keeps the interface lightweight and predictable. For example, get_user_info('john','doe',30) might return a tuple ('John Doe', 30). You can assign the returned tuple to a single variable to inspect or print it, or you can unpack it into separate variables for immediate use. A common misconception is that returning a tuple is the same as returning two separate values; technically the function returns one object — the tuple — but Python’s unpacking makes working with it feel like separate returns. Consider whether a tuple or a dictionary is better when you need named access to returned pieces, but use tuples when the returned values are positional and fixed in meaning. Unpacking is convenient: when a function returns a tuple you can assign its elements directly to variables. For example, name, years = get_user_info('jane', 'smith', 25) assigns the first element of the returned tuple to name and the second to years. This pattern keeps your caller code concise and readable. If the number of variables on the left does not match the tuple length, Python raises a ValueError, so unpack only when you know the structure. A common mistake is to assume flexible arity; tuples are fixed-length unless the function explicitly builds a variable-length tuple. In practice, use unpacking when the returned pieces have a fixed, well-known order and meaning. Be aware of two common classes of errors when working with parameters and arguments. The first is logical errors: the code runs but produces incorrect results because values were swapped or the wrong parameter was given a value. For example, swapping positional arguments in describe_pet produces misleading output. To debug, rewrite the call using keyword arguments to see which mapping produces the intended result. The second is syntax errors from mixing argument styles incorrectly; placing a positional argument after a keyword argument raises a SyntaxError, which the interpreter flags immediately. Another frequent mistake is using mutable objects as default parameter values, which can create shared state across calls; avoid this pattern unless you intentionally want that behavior. Good debugging habits include reading signatures before calls, running small test calls with explicit keywords to validate behavior, and documenting defaults in docstrings. Designing function signatures with clarity in mind prevents many of the problems we discussed. A useful pattern is to group parameters by role: required positional parameters first, then optional parameters with defaults, and finally keyword-only options if your A P I needs them. Keeping related parameters contiguous helps readers understand what values are essential and what are configurational. Document defaults in the docstring so callers know when they can omit arguments. For returned values, if you return multiple items with fixed meaning, a tuple is fine. If the returned pieces are numerous or benefit from named access, consider returning a dictionary or small object for clarity. When you review a signature, ask whether a caller can tell what to pass without reading the body. If not, revise names or add sensible defaults. This habit leads to code that is easier to use and less likely to suffer accidental misuse. Keep four ideas in mind as you use functions. First, parameters are names declared in the function signature; arguments are the actual values you pass when calling the function. Second, positional arguments match by order and are concise, but swapping them can cause logical errors. Third, keyword arguments name assignments so order does not matter and readability improves; when mixing, positionals must come first. Fourth, default parameter values provide sensible fallbacks and explicit arguments override them. Also remember that returning multiple values is commonly done with tuples and that unpacking assigns each returned element to separate variables.
